items.passage: Tehran's southern road ended where the salt flat began, and it was there my aunt took me the morning after the wedding supper. I had salted the lamb twice; I knew it the moment Bahram, our guest of honor, praised the dish and reached for his water. My aunt had tasted it too, I was certain, for her mouth tightened, yet she said nothing at table and nothing on the long drive. On the flat she bent, broke off a plate of white crust, and showed me the dark earth kept moist beneath it. Salt covers, Shirin, she said; it also keeps. I did not understand her then. I only watched her wrap the shard in her handkerchief, as carefully as she folded our best linen, and carry it home in her sleeve. The wind lifted a fine white dust across the plain, erasing our footprints behind us.
items.question: In the text, the salt crust most likely represents
options: the harsh judgment Shirin expects from her aunt after the failed wedding supper
the guest's polite pretense that the oversalted lamb had tasted good
the barren future Shirin fears if she cannot become a skilled cook
the aunt's choice to shield Shirin's error while keeping it as a lesson

items.passage:
Nothing has changed, I tell the surveyor.
I am Dolores, keeper of this Beirut court,
and every dawn I sweep the fountain's bowl
as though the water only stepped away.
Tariq writes figures in his leather book;
he does not ask why moss has turned to dust,
why coins of other summers rust and stay
unwished-upon beneath my careful broom.
We speak of walls, of tiles, of wells to dig,
and when his shadow crosses the stone lip
he steps around it, as one steps around
a sleeper no one wishes to awake.
At noon the swallows circle, find no pool,
and settle on the gate to preen and wait.
items.question: In the text, the dry fountain most likely represents
options: a loss that both Dolores and Tariq quietly avoid naming
the surveyor's plan to rebuild the courtyard into something new
Dolores's confidence that the water will soon return on its own
the ordinary decay that comes to every old building with time

items.passage: What does one do with hours that will not move? I asked myself this in the cabin above Bologna, where snow had closed the road for three days and the telegram from the hospital could not reach us. My old teacher, Moshe, spent the mornings mending a lamp whose wick had long since burned away. He trimmed a new one from a strip of his shirt, filled the reservoir, polished the glass, and then set it, unlit, on the sill facing the valley. Not yet, Assunta, he said, when I offered him a match. Each evening he wiped the frost from that pane before any other. On the fourth day a boy on skis appeared at the bend of the road, and Moshe rose so quickly that his chair fell. Pine branches shed their snow in soft collapses all around the clearing.
items.question: In the text, the unlit lamp most likely represents
options: Moshe's grief over a loss that he believes has already happened
Moshe's guarded hope, kept ready but held back until the news arrives
Assunta's impatience with her teacher's slow and stubborn habits
the cabin's isolation, which the heavy snow has made complete and lasting

items.passage: Zoya, our mother used to say, was the twin who spoke first, and Kamala the one who remembered. When we came back to the tea estate outside Dhaka to divide her bungalow, I spoke first again: I chalked a line down the veranda so each of us would know her half. By evening a rumor had reached Kamala through the plantation clerk that I meant to sell my side to the factory. She did not ask me about it. She simply moved our mother's cracked teapot, the one we had broken as girls and glued back together, from the shared shelf to her own room. I found it there the next morning, its old seam darkened with tea, a crack that had held for thirty years. Monsoon rain had already blurred my chalk line into a pale smear across the boards.
items.question: In the text, the cracked teapot most likely represents
options: Kamala's wish to keep the entire bungalow for herself after the division
the value of the estate, which the factory hopes to purchase from Zoya
the sisters' bond, once broken and repaired, now strained by the rumor
their mother's strict rules, which both daughters still obey without question

items.passage: Although the old tale says an apprentice must mend nets for seven years before she sails, I had mended them for only three when Nasrin gave me one of my own. She had worked on it, the other fishers told me, every night of the hurricane season, by the lamp at the end of the Kingston pier. Its mesh was finer than any I had seen, too fine, I thought, for the deep water I longed to fish. I wondered whether she meant it as a gift or as a tether, a net good only for the shallows near her own boat. When I asked, she laughed and said that every net catches what its maker hopes for. I hung it on my door that night and lay awake listening to it sway. Pelicans dove all morning beyond the breakwater, rising with their throats full.
items.question: In the text, the net that Nasrin makes most likely represents
options: the seven years of training the speaker must finish before she may sail
the danger of the deep water, which Nasrin herself once barely survived
the speaker's restless wish to leave the harbor and fish far offshore
a kindness the speaker suspects may also be a way to keep her nearby

items.passage: Rain dripped from the tin roof of the bus shelter in the hills above Auckland as I buttoned my mother's coat to her chin. I am Tui, and for two years I have been the one who remembers her pills, her appointments, the names of her old friends. This morning she wanted the city bus to her church, where the women still save her a seat; I had promised my new manager I would be at the clinic by nine. Her hand on my arm was a small anchor, light but certain, and I felt the whole morning swing around it. When the first bus came, I let it pass. Mist slid down the slope and settled over the empty road.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a small anchor” most nearly suggests that the mother's touch
options: drags Tui down into sadness and exhaustion
shows that the mother is frightened of the rain
holds Tui in place despite being gentle
steers Tui firmly toward her new job in the city

items.passage: Paper dust and machine oil filled the back of the rural post office outside Shanghai, where Weiqi rented a corner to sew and Nicolas, her only apprentice, pressed seams beside her. Every few days a letter arrived from the tailoring school in Lima that had accepted him, and each time Weiqi set it face down under the pincushion. Neither of them spoke of it. Their silence was a seam sewn so neatly that no stitch showed on the outside, though both could feel its ridge whenever their talk drifted toward the future. Nicolas threaded her needles before she asked; Weiqi taught him the hardest collars first. At closing, the postmaster rolled down the shutter, and bicycles rattled off into the drizzle.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a seam sewn so neatly” most nearly suggests that their silence is
options: fragile and likely to split open at any moment
comforting because they have nothing left to discuss
temporary, a habit they will soon both abandon
carefully kept, hiding a tension both still sense

items.passage: Again, from the second verse, Jordan said, leaning against the old projector in the booth above the Vermont cinema where the drama club rehearsed. Sadia, who had transferred in October and spoken perhaps forty words to her new teacher since, lowered her script but did not lift her eyes. For weeks she had treated each of his suggestions as a door she might be locked behind. Tonight, though, she asked whether she could try the line slower, and when he nodded she did, and the booth went quiet in the way rooms go quiet when something has landed. Jordan wrote nothing down. He only reached over and switched off the work light so the stage below glowed through the little window. Dust turned slowly in the beam.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a door she might be locked behind” most nearly suggests that Sadia saw Jordan's suggestions as
options: openings that would lead her toward greater success
possible traps that might confine her if she accepted
signs that Jordan wanted her to leave the drama club

items.passage: We inherited the farmhouse outside Chiang Mai the way some people inherit a quarrel: Arisa, whose father had owned the land, and I, Jiayi, whose mother had rented it for twenty years and planted every mango tree on it. A will written in two hands left it to both of us. Arisa's brother had found a buyer; my aunt wanted the trees kept. We walked the rows each evening, neither of us mentioning the price. Every tree was a ledger, I wrote that year, its rings recording the debts our families owed each other and never paid. Once Arisa pressed a palm to a trunk my mother had grafted and said nothing for a long time. In the yard, the dogs slept in the red dust beneath the water jars.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “Every tree was a ledger” most nearly suggests that the trees
options: are worth a great deal of money to the waiting buyer
remind Jiayi of the account books her mother once kept
hold a record of what each family has given and owed
have grown too old to bear much fruit any longer

items.passage: Declare anything? the customs officer, Lorenzo, asked as my mother and I reached the little checkpoint on the Cornish coast, where an old tale says brides once paid their toll in shells. My mother handed over a single photograph: her own wedding, the groom's half torn away. I had meant to show it to Callum before we chose the chapel, she told me. Lorenzo studied it and waved us through. On the cliff path she explained that the torn-away man had drowned off this coast before I was born, and that the man I called father had married her the next spring. The photograph was a locked chest washed ashore, and I could not decide whether I wanted the key. Gulls hung above the checkpoint roof, motionless against the wind.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a locked chest washed ashore” most nearly suggests that the photograph
options: is a valuable object that customs must inspect
is a burden the mother wants to be rid of at last
contains a hidden treasure that her mother hopes to sell
holds a hidden past that has surfaced unexpectedly

items.passage: Promises cost money. Aunt Consuelo said so every evening as she counted the day's coins at their food cart on the promenade in Oaxaca, and Tomoe, sixteen and tired of hearing it, had stopped arguing. That afternoon Tomoe had told a small boy, who lingered by the cart without a peso, that she would save him a tamal at closing. Consuelo had overheard and clicked her tongue. Now the sun was sinking into the Pacific, the last tamal sat wrapped in its husk, and a customer was holding out a bill for it. Consuelo took the tamal from the steamer, looked down the promenade at the boy hurrying toward them, and set it in Tomoe's hands instead. 'A promise is also a debt,' she said quietly, and for once she did not count anything.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From playful teasing to open anger, as Consuelo scolds Tomoe for giving food away.
From hopeful anticipation to disappointment, as the boy arrives too late for food.
From weary irritation to quiet tenderness, as Consuelo honors Tomoe's promise.
From calm routine to nervous urgency, as Tomoe rushes to sell out before dark.

items.passage: Krakow slid past the porthole as Harriet bent over the letter at the galley table, the only flat surface on the river barge wide enough for her pattern papers. Stanislav, her apprentice, had translated the client's instructions from Polish, and for an hour they had laughed over the request: a wedding dress cut 'short, like a quick confession.' Harriet called it the strangest order of her career and pinned the hem a scandalous hand above the knee. Then Stanislav, rereading the original, went pale. The word he had rendered as 'short' could also mean 'plain,' and the bride, whose mother had died that spring, wanted nothing that would draw the eye. Harriet set the scissors down without a word and began, slowly, to unpick every pin.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From quiet concentration to frantic panic, as Harriet fears missing a deadline.
From mutual suspicion to trust, as Harriet comes to rely on Stanislav's skill.
From cheerful pride to defiance, as Harriet refuses to change her own design.
From amused curiosity to sober regret, as the error alters the dress's meaning.

items.passage:
'Check,' Maya said, though no board lay between us,
only the boarding-house kettle and two cracked cups.
All week the club had whispered of my blunder,
the queen I'd left hanging like wash in the Haifa wind,
and Maya, smug as a bishop, had told it best.
So I, Dvora, came down to the kitchen armed with silence,
ready to answer every pawn of her pity.
But she poured the tea, and slid the sugar toward me,
and said she'd lost the same way once, at twenty,
to a man who never let her forget it.
We sat until the window went blue with morning,
two old rivals, the game between us set down.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the poem?
options: From wary defensiveness to reconciliation, as the rival offers unexpected sympathy.
From triumph to humiliation, as the speaker loses a second game to her rival.
From nostalgia to bitterness, as the speaker recalls a man who mocked her.
From playful banter to cold politeness, as both women hide their true feelings.

items.passage:
'I keep telling you, Pa, nobody pays for hand-pressing anymore,' CLEMENT says, dropping a basket onto the folding counter of the laundromat in Port of Spain. LINTON, his father, does not answer. He lifts an old charcoal iron from its shelf and sets it heating.
CLEMENT: You'll burn the place down with that relic.
LINTON: (smoothing a white collar) Your grandmother pressed shirts for half of Belmont with this. Every crease told the customer somebody cared.
CLEMENT: (mocking) Every crease told them she couldn't afford a machine.
(LINTON holds out the iron. CLEMENT hesitates, then takes it. He presses one sleeve, clumsy at first, then slower, then slower still.)
CLEMENT: (quietly) It's heavier than I thought.
LINTON: That's the weight of it. She carried it up every hill in Belmont.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From warm nostalgia to open grief, as Linton mourns his late mother aloud.
From scornful dismissal to grudging respect, as Clement feels the craft's weight.
From playful joking to sharp anger, as Linton scolds Clement's clumsiness.
From quiet tension to relief, as Clement agrees to replace the old iron.

items.passage: Two bowls of miso ramen steamed between us in the roadside diner outside Asahikawa, and for the first twenty minutes Judge Sota talked only about procedure. I had clerked for him for three years, and he reminded me that he had misspelled my name, Rohan, on my first evaluation; he wanted to correct the record before he left Hokkaido for good. He listed the filing deadlines I would need to watch under his successor, the drawer that stuck, the bailiff who hated small talk. Then a snowplow rumbled past the window and he stopped mid-sentence. 'I was not a kind judge,' he said, looking at his noodles. 'I hope I was a fair one. You will have to tell me which matters more.' I saw that he had driven three hours not to brief me but to be judged.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From cheerful nostalgia to resentment over the narrator's first evaluation.
From awkward silence to lively debate about the judge's chosen successor.
From brisk, practical instruction to vulnerable self-examination by the judge.
From formal reserve to playful teasing as the judge mocks the old bailiff.

items.passage: Caio came back on a Tuesday. I was working the night shift at the customs checkpoint outside Vienna, as I had since renting him the flat above my bakery eleven years before, and there he was in the queue, his passport held out as if no time had passed. For four years his rent had arrived each month by mail, no letter attached, while his rooms sat dark. I had rehearsed a speech for this moment: the questions, the overdue repairs, the neighbors' rumors. I stamped his passport with exaggerated care. Then he set something on the counter: the spare key I had given him, wrapped in a handkerchief my mother had embroidered, which I thought had been lost with her belongings. 'She asked me to keep it safe, Lena,' he said. My speech went somewhere I could not follow.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From cheerful surprise to suspicion, as the narrator questions Caio's passport.
From weary routine to anger, as the narrator delivers her rehearsed speech.
From anxious fear to relief, as Caio finally pays all of the overdue rent.
From guarded resentment to stunned emotion, as Caio reveals a tie to her mother.

items.passage:
Years ago, Achan, you stood with me on our rooftop in Kochi, pinning your work shirts to the line, and told me never to explain our move to Aigerim until she was old enough. I agreed; I was twelve and proud to keep a secret in a language you were still learning. Now Aigerim is ten, and she asks me in English why we left, and I answer her in the cheerful phrases you approved: better schools, a bigger sky. But last week she found your old visa papers folded in the laundry basket, the ones stamped refused twice, and she asked me why you had cried on the phone. I could not invent a cheerful phrase for that. She deserves the true version, told by you, and I am asking you to tell her.
With love, Ananya
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the letter?
options: From fond recollection of a shared promise to an earnest appeal to break it.
From cheerful description to bitter accusation that the father lied to them.
From formal politeness to playful humor about Aigerim's curious questions.
From anxious worry to calm relief, as Ananya resolves to keep the secret.

items.passage: 'Read the harbor part again,' Yuxuan said, and so I did, sitting cross-legged among the half-strung kites in the old kite-maker's yard in Lisbon where Mother used to work. Our plan had been simple: sell her last kites at the festival, use the money to buy back the letters she had pawned, and finally learn why she left for those three years. Today the plan worked. We sold all nine kites before noon. We bought the bundle back, tied in her blue thread, and we laughed the whole way to the yard. Then we read them. She wrote about the harbor, about missing us, about a doctor she never mentioned. Yuxuan has folded the letters back into their thread. Neither of us has said a word since. I wanted answers; I did not know they would weigh this much. Shanice, before bed
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the diary entry?
options: From quiet grief to renewed hope as the siblings recover their mother's letters.
From buoyant excitement over a successful plan to a heavy, subdued silence.
From anxious doubt to pride as the siblings sell every kite before noon.
From playful teasing to open conflict as Yuxuan refuses to hear the letters.

items.passage: Who remembers when the old piano first lost its voice? In a school music room in Surabaya, so the story goes, two friends named Zofia and Thuy played duets on it every afternoon from the time they were small, one on the high keys, one on the low. They rarely spoke; the music did their talking. Each year another key went silent, and each year they simply played around the gap, inventing new harmonies, pretending nothing was missing. Children came to listen and clapped at the clever detours. One afternoon only a single key still sounded. Thuy pressed it, and Zofia pressed it after her, and they kept trading that one note, softer and softer, until the bell rang and neither lifted her hand from the keys.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From eager rivalry to cooperation, as the friends stop competing for keys.
From joyful celebration to bitter anger, as the piano is finally removed.
From lighthearted ingenuity in avoiding loss to a solemn acceptance of it.
From deep sadness to cheerful hope, as children gather to applaud the pair.
